name: 1946 GLE #3

phenomena.details: First recognised ground-level enhancement, recorded at Cheltenham and Climax neutron monitors. Established the GLE catalogue.
Associated large solar flare; detailed observations limited for this period.
High-energy solar energetic particles reaching ground level via secondary cosmic ray cascade.

impacts.description: Elevated radiation dose to aircraft passengers and crew at high altitudes; not recognised as a hazard at the time but now understood to represent a significant radiation environment (no proton-flux measurements exist for 1946, so no NOAA S-scale is assigned).

papers.title: Three Unusual Cosmic-Ray Increases Possibly Due to Charged Particles from the Sun
papers.keyFinding: First documentation of a solar-associated increase in ground-level cosmic ray flux, establishing the concept of the ground-level enhancement.

papers.title: Re-examination of the First Five Ground-Level Events
papers.journal: Proceedings of 36th International Cosmic Ray Conference — PoS(ICRC2019)
papers.keyFinding: Re-examined the first five ground-level events (1942–1956), including 25 July 1946 (GLE 3), using the original ionisation-chamber records.

summary: The 25 July 1946 solar cosmic-ray increase – GLE #3 in the modern catalogue, after the two 1942 events – was recorded by Scott Forbush's ionisation chambers and helped establish that the Sun can accelerate particles to GeV energies.
description: Scott Forbush's ionisation chambers at Cheltenham (Maryland), Christchurch (New Zealand) and Godhavn (Greenland) registered a sudden increase in cosmic-ray intensity on 25 July 1946, following a large solar flare. Together with the two increases of 28 February and 7 March 1942, Forbush (1946) argued the particles came from the Sun – the first identification of solar cosmic rays. The three events are numbered GLE #1, #2 and #3 in the modern ground-level enhancement catalogue, which by 2025 exceeded 75 events; the 1946 event is the third, not the first, and predates the neutron-monitor era (Climax, the first monitor, opened in 1951). Its scientific significance lies not in its intensity – later GLEs have been far larger – but in establishing that solar energetic particles can reach ground level.
